examples: I'm from Slovakia.
My sister is a doctor.
note: Ser: who or what something is, origin, profession, characteristics (Soy de Eslovaquia). Estar: where something is and how someone is doing (Estoy en casa, Estoy cansado).

examples: How are you?
The bathroom is on the right.
note: Estar: location and temporary states (Estoy en casa, Estoy cansado). Compare with ser.

examples: I'm thirty years old.
Tomorrow I have to work.
note: Age: Tengo 30 años = I'm 30 years old. Tener que + infinitive = to have to: Tengo que trabajar.

examples: I'm going to the market.
Shall we go to the beach on Saturday?
note: Ir a + infinitive expresses the future: Voy a comer = I'm going to eat.

examples: What are you doing?
It's very cold today.
note: Weather: Hace calor = It's hot, Hace frío = It's cold.

examples: Do you speak English?
I speak a little Spanish.
Where are we having lunch today?
note: In Mexico “comer” often means to have lunch (the main meal of the day).

examples: We live in an apartment downtown.
I work in an office.
Do you want a coffee?
I want to go to the beach.
note: Te quiero = I love you (to family, friends and a partner).

examples: Can I pay by card?
What time does the bus arrive?
I got to work late.
note: The spelling changes in the preterite: llegué (to keep the sound of the “g”).

examples: I'm going to buy tortillas.
What do you want to drink?
I take the subway every day.
note: In Mexico: tomar agua = to drink water, tomar el camión = to take the bus. Don't use the verb “coger” in Mexico: it's vulgar.

examples: I leave work at six.
Shall we go out on Friday?
Are you coming to the party?
note: Venir = to come here, toward the speaker. Llegar = to arrive somewhere.

examples: What did the doctor say?
I like chatting with my grandma.
note: A typically Mexican word for “to chat”. In Spain more often “charlar”.

examples: What's your name?
My name is Adam.
I slept very well last night.
I study Spanish every day.
note: estudiar = to study (a subject); aprender = to learn something.

examples: I walk to work because it's close.
My dad cooks on Sundays.
I have to clean the kitchen.
I like listening to music on the bus.
What are you looking at?
note: For television, Mexicans usually say “ver la tele”.

examples: I need help, please.
I'll wait for you at the entrance.
note: esperar = to wait and also to hope: Espero que sí. = I hope so.

examples: Will you help me with the suitcases?
Do you want to dance?
My sister sings beautifully.
We want to travel to Oaxaca in December.
Do you know how to drive?
note: In Mexico it's “manejar” (in Spain “conducir”).

examples: Can I use your computer?
I'll take this shirt.
Today I'm wearing a jacket.
note: In a store, “Me lo llevo” = I'll take it.

examples: Can I ask you something?
note: preguntar = to ask a question; pedir = to ask for something.

examples: He isn't answering the phone.
What time does the class end?
I'll be back at eight.
note: In Mexico usually “regresar” (in Spain more often “volver”).

examples: Today I want to rest at home.
I'm going to wash the dishes.
I'm making dinner.
How much do you earn a month?
note: ganar = to earn and also to win: ganar el partido.

examples: We want to rent an apartment near the beach.
note: In Mexico it's “rentar” (in Spain “alquilar”).

examples: I love swimming in the sea.
I always forget my keys.
note: In everyday speech people often say “Se me olvidó” = I forgot.

examples: What do you usually have for breakfast?
We have dinner at nine.
On Saturday we're visiting my grandparents.
May I come in?
I'll call you later.
note: llamar = to call, to phone; llamarse = to be called.

examples: What happened?
We spent the weekend at the beach.
I left my phone at home.
Where can I park the car?
note: In Mexico it's “estacionar” (in Spain “aparcar”).

examples: I miss you a lot.
note: Extraño a mi familia = I miss my family.

examples: We caught the subway downtown.
note: Common in Mexico (instead of “coger”, which is vulgar here).

examples: I'll pay the check.
note: Preterite: pagué (the “u” keeps the sound of the “g”).

examples: I'm looking for my glasses.
note: Preterite: busqué.

examples: I've played the guitar since I was a kid.
note: tocar = to play an instrument; jugar = to play a game or a sport.

examples: I practice Spanish with my friends.
I'm going to check my email.
note: Typically Mexican (from English “check”). Preterite: chequé.

examples: The movie starts at seven.
What do you think?
note: pensar en = to think about; pensar + infinitive = to plan to: Pienso viajar.

examples: What time does the bank close?
I can't find my passport.
How much does it cost?
note: Used mostly in the 3rd person: cuesta (one thing), cuestan (several things).

examples: I don't remember his name.
note: A false friend: recordar = to remember; to record = grabar.

en: to play (a game or a sport)
examples: The kids play soccer in the park.
note: In Mexico it's “jugar fútbol”, with no “al”. Preterite: jugué.

examples: Do you want to try the tacos?
note: probarse = to try on (clothes).

examples: I get up early.
I shower in the morning.
note: In Mexico “bañarse” = to take a shower as well as a bath.

examples: Today I'm staying home.
I wake up at six.
I go to bed late on Fridays.
Can I sit here?
My boss got very angry.
note: In Mexico it's “enojarse” (in Spain more often “enfadarse”).

examples: Don't worry.
I got sick last week.
Will you give me your number?
I drink a lot of water.
note: In Mexico people more often say “tomar” for drinks.

examples: I want to learn Spanish.
I run in the park on Saturdays.
They sell fruit at the market.
I like to read before going to sleep.
I don't understand. Could you repeat that, please?
I lost my phone.
note: perder el camión = to miss the bus; perder el partido = to lose the game.

examples: When are you coming back?
note: volver a + infinitive = to do something again: Volví a llamar = I called again.

examples: I don't know.
Do you know how to swim?
note: saber = to know (a fact, a skill); conocer = to know (a person, a place).

examples: Do you know my sister?
note: Before a person it takes “a”: conocer a alguien.

examples: Where do I put the keys?
Will you bring me a glass of water?
We're going to watch a movie.
I'll write you a message.
The store opens at ten.
We get on the bus at the corner.
note: subir = to go up, to get on; bajar = to go down, to get off.

examples: I'm going to order some tacos.
note: pedir = to order, to ask for something; preguntar = to ask a question.

examples: Could you repeat that, please?
How do you feel?
I prefer coffee without sugar.
We had a lot of fun at the party.
We have to make the most of the nice weather.
Can I exchange this T-shirt for another size?
note: cambiar dinero = to exchange money; cambiarse = to change clothes.

examples: I share the apartment with two friends.
I'll send you the photo on WhatsApp.
note: In Mexico more common than “enviar”. ¿Mande? = Pardon? (when you didn't hear something).

examples: I spend a lot of money on food.
I'm going to try again.
I managed to finish the project on time.
Tomorrow I turn thirty.
note: cumplir años = to have a birthday; cumplir una promesa = to keep a promise.

examples: I'm saving for a car.
I just got here.
note: acabar de + infinitive = to have just done something.

examples: Turn on the light, please.
note: Mexican; in Spain “encender”.

examples: Let me know when you get here.
What did you get for your birthday?
My siblings are always fighting.
Flip the tortilla.
note: Mexican. voltear a ver = to turn and look.

examples: We moved to Guadalajara last year.
My neighbor is always complaining about the noise.
My sister got married in December.
note: casarse con alguien = to marry someone.

examples: Can you explain it to me again?
Can you take a picture of us?
note: sacar dinero = to take out money; sacar la basura = to take out the trash.

examples: Turn off the TV, it's late.
I grew up in a small town near Puebla.
They offered me a job in Monterrey.
It seems like a good idea to me.
note: Me parece que… = it seems to me that…; parecerse a alguien = to look like someone.

examples: I think you're right.
I fell off my bike.
note: Without “se”: caer = to fall (la lluvia cae). Me cae bien = I like him (as a person).

examples: They're building a new hospital.
Do you remember me?
note: acordarse de algo = to remember something; recordar algo means the same without “de”.

examples: Is someone helping you already?
note: A false friend: to attend (a class, an event) = asistir a.

examples: I finally got a job.
Keep going straight for two blocks.
I still work at the same place.
note: seguir + gerund = to keep doing something, to still be doing it.

examples: I don't know what to choose.
This charger doesn't work.
note: In Mexico: no sirve = it doesn't work, it's broken.

examples: He always tells the truth; he never lies.
My grandpa died two years ago.
note: Colloquially: me muero de hambre = I'm starving.

examples: Can you translate this message for me?
How are you doing?
I'm very tired this week.
note: Very common in Mexico: ¿Cómo andas? = How are you doing?; ando + gerund = I'm doing something right now.

examples: Tell me what happened.
My son already knows how to count to a hundred.
Can you show me the way to the subway?
My grandma taught me to cook.
note: To teach someone = enseñar; to learn = aprender.

examples: Did you get my message?
We haven't decided yet where to go on vacation.
Let me buy you a coffee.
note: “Te invito” usually means that I'm paying too.

examples: The technician is going to fix the washing machine tomorrow.

examples: Here's an idea: let's go to the beach on Saturday.
note: Conjugated like poner: propongo, propuse, propondré.

examples: I can't reach the top shelf.
Do you have enough money?
note: In Mexico often “to be enough”: no me alcanza = I don't have enough (money, time).
